en: To make something more noticeable or prominent; to emphasize
hook: ACCENTUATE: put an ACCENT on it to make it stand out.
story: Accentuate. Before her friend's wedding, Mitu lined her eyes with dark kajal. Suddenly her large brown eyes were the first thing everyone noticed. The next day, writing her research report, she used bold headings and a single bright chart so that her key finding jumped off the page. Both times, she accentuated something: made it more noticeable, emphasized it. Dim lighting accentuates a room's warmth; a crisis can accentuate inequality. Think: put an accent on it.

gre.s: The designer used dark frames and bright lighting to ____ the paintings' vivid colors, making them seem to glow against the gray walls.
gre.clue: making them seem to glow

en: Based on guesswork or incomplete information
hook: CONJECTURE = a guess. CONJECTURAL = guess-based.
story: Conjectural. Professor Haque held up a broken clay pot. "This belonged to a king who ruled here two thousand years ago," he said. "I believe he died in battle." A student asked how he knew. He smiled. "I do not know. No written records survive. My account is conjectural, pieced together from coins, pots, and guesswork." Conjectural means based on guesswork or incomplete evidence. A conjecture is a guess. GRE passages contrast conjectural theories with empirical proof.

gre.s: Because no fossils from the period have been found, any account of the species' behavior must remain largely ____.
gre.clue: no fossils from the period have been found

en: Friendly, lively, and enjoyable; fond of good company
hook: CON-VIVIAL: 'vivi' means life. Full of lively company.
story: Convivial. Every Eid, Uncle Rahim's house overflows. Cousins laugh in every corner. The elders tell the same old stories, and everyone laughs anyway. Music drifts from a phone speaker, plates of biryani keep refilling, and nobody checks the time. Guests who planned to stay one hour leave after six. The atmosphere is convivial: friendly, lively, and enjoyable. Vivi means life, as in vivid. A convivial host makes every guest feel welcome.

gre.s: Although the conference sessions were tense, the evening banquets were ____ affairs, full of laughter and lively conversation.
gre.clue: full of laughter and lively conversation

en: Marked by moral decline and excessive self-indulgence
hook: DECADENT: DECAYING morals.
story: Decadent. In the final years of the empire, the nobles threw parties that lasted for days. Golden plates. Rivers of wine. Musicians playing until dawn. Meanwhile, outside the palace walls, farmers starved and soldiers went unpaid. Within a decade, the empire collapsed. Historians describe that court as decadent: marked by moral decline and excessive indulgence in luxury. Decadent shares a root with decay. Today people jokingly call a rich chocolate cake decadent.

gre.s: Moralists of the era denounced the city's nightlife as ____, a sign that luxury and pleasure had corrupted the nation's character.
gre.clue: luxury and pleasure had corrupted the nation's character

en: Outstandingly bad; shocking
hook: EGREGIOUS: so bad it stands out from the herd (e-greg = out of the flock).
story: Egregious. In the final minute of the match, the striker tumbled to the ground in the penalty box. The referee pointed to the spot. Penalty. But the replay showed clearly that no defender had touched him; he had simply thrown himself down. Millions of viewers screamed at their TVs. The error was egregious: shockingly, glaringly bad. Egregious comes from the Latin for standing out from the flock. An egregious mistake is not small; it is outrageous.

gre.s: The auditors uncovered an ____ error in the accounts, a miscalculation so large that it had inflated profits by millions.
gre.clue: so large that it had inflated profits by millions

en: Quickly fading or disappearing
hook: EVANESCENT: EVAPORATES and VANISHES.
story: Evanescent. After a sudden shower over the Padma, a rainbow arched across the sky, so bright it seemed painted. Arif scrambled for his phone. By the time he unlocked it, the colours were already fading. By the time he opened the camera, the sky was plain grey again. The rainbow had been evanescent: quickly fading and disappearing. Think: it evaporates and vanishes. Evanescent, ephemeral, and transient all describe things that do not last.

gre.s: The perfume's scent proved ____, fading within minutes of being applied despite the manufacturer's promise that it would last all day.
gre.clue: fading within minutes

en: Very confident, showy, and colorful in a way that attracts attention
hook: FLAMBOYANT: like FLAMES, bright and impossible to ignore.
story: Flamboyant. At the awards night, most guests wore black. Then the singer arrived: a gold jacket, purple feathers on his shoulders, sunglasses studded with sparkling stones, and boots that lit up with every step. He blew kisses to the crowd and twirled for the cameras. Every lens turned toward him. He was flamboyant: confident, showy, and colourful in a way that demands attention. Think of flames, bright and impossible to ignore.

gre.s: Unlike her ____ predecessor, who favored sequined gowns and dramatic entrances, the new director dresses plainly and avoids the spotlight.
gre.clue: who favored sequined gowns and dramatic entrances

en: To prevent or hinder something by acting in advance
hook: FORE-STALL: act BEFOREhand to STALL it.
story: Forestall. The vice-chancellor heard that students were planning a massive protest against the fee increase on Monday morning. On Sunday night, he called a press conference and announced a new scholarship fund that would cover the increase for every poor student. Monday came, and nobody protested. His quick move had forestalled the protest: prevented it by acting in advance. Think: act before, and stall it. Vaccines forestall epidemics.

gre.s: The company hoped to ____ a hostile takeover by buying back its own shares before the rival bid could be launched.
gre.clue: before the rival bid could be launched

en: To deny or contradict
hook: GAINSAY: to say AGAINST.
story: Gainsay. The evidence against the thief was overwhelming: CCTV footage, his fingerprints on the safe, and three witnesses who saw him running away. His lawyer stood up, opened her mouth, then closed it again. Nobody could gainsay the facts. To gainsay is to deny or contradict something. It is usually used with a negative: "There is no gainsaying her talent" means her talent is undeniable. Think: to say against.

gre.s: No one could ____ the champion's skill; even her fiercest critics admitted that she was the finest player of her generation.
gre.clue: even her fiercest critics admitted

en: To shock or excite someone into taking action
hook: GALVANIZE: Galvani made dead frog legs jump with electricity.
story: Galvanize. A single photograph went viral one morning: a small girl standing on a flooded rooftop, holding her baby brother above the brown water. Within hours, the whole country was moving. Students collected boats. Restaurants cooked thousands of meals. Strangers donated millions of taka. The photo had galvanized the nation: shocked and excited it into action. The word comes from Galvani, a scientist who made frogs' legs twitch with electric current.

gre.s: The activist's passionate speech seemed to ____ the previously apathetic crowd, which immediately began organizing marches.
gre.clue: previously apathetic crowd, which immediately began organizing

en: Done at random or without careful judgment
hook: IN-DISCRIMINATE: doesn't DISCRIMINATE, doesn't choose carefully.
story: Indiscriminate. Worried about pests, a farmer sprayed pesticide over his entire field, the pond, the trees, and the nearby hedges. He killed the pests. He also killed the bees, the frogs, the birds, and every fish in the pond. His spraying had been indiscriminate: done at random, without careful judgment or selection. In means not, discriminate means to distinguish carefully. Indiscriminate use of antibiotics creates superbugs that no medicine can kill.

gre.s: Critics condemned the ____ bombing campaign, which struck hospitals and markets as readily as military targets.
gre.clue: struck hospitals and markets as readily as military targets

en: Not harmful or offensive
hook: IN-NOCUOUS: not NOXIOUS, harmless.
story: Innocuous. At the family dinner, Sara asked her cousin a simple, friendly question: "So, when is the wedding?" She expected a date and a smile. Instead, her cousin burst into tears and ran upstairs. The engagement had been cancelled that morning. Sara's question had seemed innocuous: harmless and inoffensive. Most garden snakes look frightening but are innocuous. In means not, nocuous means harmful, as in noxious.

gre.s: What seemed an ____ comment about the budget was interpreted by the minister as a direct attack and provoked a furious response.
gre.clue: was interpreted by the minister as a direct attack

en: Lasting for a very short time
hook: MOMENTARY: lasts a MOMENT.
story: Momentary. The teacher unfolded the results sheet and cleared her throat. "The top scorer this year is…" There was a momentary silence, so tense you could hear the ceiling fan, and then she read Ishita's name and the whole class erupted in cheers. Momentary means lasting only a moment. A momentary lapse in concentration on the highway can cause a crash. Momentary hesitation, momentary panic, momentary silence: brief and quickly gone.

gre.s: The pilot's ____ lapse in concentration lasted only a second, but it was long enough to put the plane dangerously off course.
gre.clue: lasted only a second

en: Ordinary and lacking interest or excitement
hook: MUNDANE: MONDAY-ish, ordinary routine.
story: Mundane. Kids imagine astronauts spend all day floating dramatically past windows and fixing satellites. In reality, much of their work is mundane: cleaning air filters, logging data on laptops, running on a treadmill for two hours to keep their bones strong. Even in space, there are chores. Mundane means ordinary, dull, and routine. It can also mean worldly, as opposed to spiritual. Mundane sounds like Monday: the start of another ordinary week.

gre.s: The novelist has a gift for transforming ____ events, such as a trip to the grocery store, into moments of startling beauty.
gre.clue: such as a trip to the grocery store

en: Causing annoyance or difficulty
hook: NETTLE is a stinging plant. NETTLESOME = stings and annoys.
story: Nettlesome. One mosquito. That was all. It found Tanvir at midnight and buzzed around his ear. He switched on the light; it vanished. He switched it off; it returned. Slap. Miss. Buzz. By three in the morning, he was itchy, furious, and wide awake. That tiny insect was nettlesome: causing annoyance or difficulty. A nettle is a plant that stings when touched. A nettlesome problem keeps stinging you, no matter how you try to ignore it.

gre.s: The software update was meant to fix a ____ glitch that had irritated users for months, causing the screen to freeze at random.
gre.clue: that had irritated users for months

en: To make legally invalid; to cancel out the effect of
hook: NULLIFY: make it NULL, zero.
story: Nullify. After the election, investigators found that thousands of votes had been cast by people who did not exist. The court ruled the whole result invalid, and the election was held again. The court had nullified it: made it legally void, as if it had never happened. Nullify also means to cancel out an effect: three plates of biryani after the gym can nullify your entire workout. Think: make it null, zero.

gre.s: The appeals court moved to ____ the contract, ruling that it had been signed under duress and was therefore void.
gre.clue: was therefore void

en: To remove a need or difficulty; to make unnecessary
hook: OBVIATE: OBVIOUSLY not needed anymore.
story: Obviate. Every month, Rafi's father used to take a day off work to stand in a long bank queue to pay the electricity, gas, and water bills. Then he learned mobile banking. Now he pays everything from his phone in two minutes while drinking tea. The new system obviated the need for the queue: it removed the need entirely. To obviate is to make something unnecessary. A GPS obviates the need for paper maps.

gre.s: The new vaccine, if effective, would ____ the need for the costly and painful treatments currently used to fight the disease.
gre.clue: the need for the costly and painful treatments

en: Present everywhere at the same time
hook: OMNI = all, PRESENT = there. Present everywhere.
story: Omnipresent. During the election season, one candidate's face was everywhere: on posters on every wall, on billboards above every road, on rickshaws, on tea cups, on the back of buses, even printed on balloons for children. Joya joked that she saw him more often than her own family. He was omnipresent: present everywhere at once. Omni means all. In religion, God is described as omnipresent. It is a synonym of ubiquitous.

gre.s: In the city's busiest district, security cameras are virtually ____, mounted on nearly every corner and doorway.
gre.clue: mounted on nearly every corner and doorway

en: To force someone out of a position or place
hook: OUST: kick OUT.
story: Oust. For five straight years, the company lost money. Products failed. Staff quit. Investors grew furious. Finally, at a tense board meeting, the directors voted to remove the CEO, and security escorted him out of the building that same afternoon. He had been ousted: forced out of his position against his will. Think: kicked out. Popular movements have ousted many rulers throughout history; shareholders can oust a failing executive.

gre.s: The rebels' attempt to ____ the dictator failed when the army remained loyal to him.
gre.clue: when the army remained loyal to him

en: So intense or obvious that it can almost be touched or felt
hook: PALPABLE: you can PALPATE it, touch it with your hand.
story: Palpable. In the coaching centre, forty students waited for their official GRE scores to load on the screen. Nobody spoke. Nobody moved. Someone's leg bounced nervously under a desk. You could almost reach out and touch the tension in the air. It was palpable: so intense or obvious that it can almost be physically felt. Doctors palpate, or touch, a body to examine it. Palpable relief, palpable excitement, palpable fear.

gre.s: As the verdict was read, the courtroom's tension was ____, and several spectators visibly held their breath.
gre.clue: several spectators visibly held their breath

en: Deceitfulness; betrayal of trust
hook: PERFIDY: per-FID-y, breaking FIDelity (faithfulness).
story: Perfidy. In 1757, at the Battle of Plassey, Nawab Siraj-ud-Daulah trusted his commander, Mir Jafar, to lead a large part of his army. Mir Jafar had secretly made a deal with the British. On the battlefield, his troops simply stood still. The Nawab lost, and Bengal fell under British control. Mir Jafar's perfidy is remembered to this day: deliberate betrayal of trust. In Bangladesh, his name itself means traitor.

gre.s: The spy's ____ came to light only after his death, when documents revealed that he had sold his country's secrets for decades.
gre.clue: sold his country's secrets for decades

en: Abundant; flowing out in great quantity
hook: PROFUSE: PRO + FUSE, pouring forth in a flood.
story: Profuse. At the host's dinner party, Farhan stood up too fast and knocked a crystal vase off the table. It shattered. He went red. "I am so sorry! So, so sorry! I will pay for it! I am really very sorry!" The next morning he arrived with flowers and apologized again. His apologies were profuse: pouring out in great quantity. Profuse sweating, profuse bleeding, profuse thanks. Think of something fused and flowing out abundantly.

gre.s: The patient's ____ bleeding, which continued despite pressure on the wound, alarmed the emergency team.
gre.clue: which continued despite pressure on the wound

en: Eager or quick to argue, quarrel, or fight
hook: PUGNACIOUS: ready to throw a PUNCH, like a pug that barks at everyone.
story: Pugnacious. Everyone at the tea stall knew Uncle Selim. Say one wrong word about his cricket team, and he would start shouting. A rickshaw brushed his car? He jumped out with his fists up. Once he argued with a parrot. People learned to agree with him about everything. He was pugnacious: eager and quick to argue, quarrel, or fight. Pugnus is Latin for fist, as in pugilist, a boxer. Picture a tiny pug barking at everyone.

gre.s: The usually ____ senator surprised observers by conceding the point calmly instead of launching into one of his customary attacks.
gre.clue: instead of launching into one of his customary attacks

en: Having or showing keen wisdom and good judgment
hook: SAGACIOUS: a wise SAGE.
story: Sagacious. Two families in the village had argued over a strip of land for three years. Lawyers had failed. Police had failed. Finally they visited the old imam, a man known across the district for his wisdom. He listened patiently to both sides for an hour, asked three simple questions, and proposed a solution that both families accepted with relief. He was sagacious: wise and shrewd, with keen judgment. Think of a sage.

gre.s: Investors trusted the ____ banker, whose cautious predictions had been proved correct through three market crashes.
gre.clue: whose cautious predictions had been proved correct through three market crashes

en: Optimistic, especially in a difficult situation
hook: SANGUINE: 'sanguis' is blood. Rosy-cheeked, full of hope.
story: Sanguine. Rafi's flight to Toronto was cancelled. Then the airline lost his luggage. Then it started raining, and his phone died. His travelling companion was in tears. Rafi just smiled and bought two cups of tea. "We will get tomorrow's flight. The bag will turn up. It is fine." He was sanguine: confidently optimistic, especially in a difficult situation. Sanguis is Latin for blood: imagine rosy, healthy cheeks full of hope.

gre.s: Despite the grim forecasts, the finance minister remained ____ about the economy, predicting a strong recovery by the end of the year.
gre.clue: predicting a strong recovery

en: Barely sufficient; very little
hook: SCANT: SCANTY, hardly enough.
story: Scant. Tanvir bought a flat-pack bookshelf and threw the instruction booklet aside after one glance. Two hours later, the shelf leaned sideways, a drawer would not close, and three screws lay mysteriously on the floor. He had paid scant attention to the instructions: barely any at all. Scant means barely sufficient, very little. There is scant evidence for many viral health claims. Scant rainfall warns farmers that a drought may be coming.

gre.s: The theory has attracted wide popular attention despite ____ evidence, resting on a single study that has never been replicated.
gre.clue: resting on a single study that has never been replicated

en: Underhanded, dishonest, or deceptive behavior
hook: SKULL-DUGGERY: digging up skulls at night; secret, shady business.
story: Skullduggery. The election for club president was a mess. Fake members suddenly appeared on the voter list. Secret deals were struck in back rooms. A ballot box mysteriously vanished for an hour and came back heavier. The losing candidate demanded an investigation into the skullduggery: underhanded, dishonest, sneaky behaviour. Picture someone digging up skulls at midnight; that is the shady feeling of the word. Political thrillers are packed with skullduggery.

gre.s: The merger was finalized only after months of ____, including leaked documents, secret side deals, and bribed officials.
gre.clue: leaked documents, secret side deals, and bribed officials

en: Of little value or importance
hook: TRIVIAL: like TRIVIA, small unimportant facts.
story: Trivial. Mitu and her best friend did not speak for an entire week. The cause? An argument over whose turn it was to pay for two cups of tea at the campus stall. Twenty taka. When they finally made up, they laughed until they cried at how unimportant it had been. It was trivial: of little value or importance. Trivia are small, unimportant facts. In an exam, do not waste time on trivial details.

gre.s: Although the error seemed ____ at the time, a mere decimal point out of place, it eventually cost the company millions.
gre.clue: it eventually cost the company millions

en: Designed to be useful and practical rather than attractive
hook: UTILITARIAN: all about UTILITY (usefulness).
story: Utilitarian. The new university hostel had no paintings, no carpets, no decorations at all. Plain concrete walls. Metal bunk beds. Simple wooden desks. Bright white tube lights. But everything worked perfectly: hot water, fast Wi-Fi, strong locks. It was utilitarian: designed to be useful and practical rather than attractive. Think: all about utility. In philosophy, utilitarianism judges actions by how much good they do for the greatest number of people.

gre.s: The factory's ____ design, which prioritized efficiency over appearance, made it one of the least attractive buildings in the city.
gre.clue: prioritized efficiency over appearance

en: Offering nothing stimulating or challenging; dull and empty
hook: VAPID: like VAPOR, empty air.
story: Vapid. The TV channel interviewed a famous actor for twenty minutes. Every answer was the same: "I just love my fans." "I am so blessed." "It was an amazing experience." Not one thought, not one opinion, not one interesting detail. Viewers switched channels. The interview was vapid: dull, empty, and lacking anything stimulating. Think of vapour: just empty air. Vapid is a close synonym of insipid.

gre.s: The critic dismissed the pop song's lyrics as ____, a string of empty phrases that said nothing at all about love.
gre.clue: a string of empty phrases that said nothing at all
